questions.question: In the standard mixed‑precision training workflow, what is the primary role of maintaining FP32 "master weights"?
questions.choice_A: To enable model parallelism across devices by storing replicas
questions.choice_B: To apply precise optimizer updates while performing forward/backward compute in lower precision
questions.choice_C: To cache activations for gradient checkpointing without recomputation
questions.choice_D: To reduce memory fragmentation caused by dynamic shapes

questions.question: Which statement best characterizes BF16 compared to FP16 for training deep networks?
questions.choice_A: BF16 has more mantissa bits and less exponent range than FP16, reducing underflow
questions.choice_B: BF16 has fewer mantissa and exponent bits than FP16, so it generally needs more loss scaling
questions.choice_C: BF16 and FP16 have identical numerical properties; the choice is purely hardware‑driven
questions.choice_D: BF16 has the same exponent range as FP32 but fewer mantissa bits than FP16, often avoiding loss scaling

questions.question: Why are FP32 master weights typically updated even when forward/backward are computed in FP16/BF16?
questions.choice_A: Because small gradient updates may be lost in low precision due to limited mantissa, harming convergence
questions.choice_B: Because optimizers cannot read low‑precision tensors in current frameworks
questions.choice_C: Because low‑precision compute cannot represent negative values reliably
questions.choice_D: Because batch normalization requires FP32 parameters by design

questions.question: Dynamic loss scaling is primarily designed to do which of the following during mixed‑precision training?
questions.choice_A: Increase the learning rate adaptively in response to vanishing gradients
questions.choice_B: Quantize gradients to FP8 during communication while keeping local FP32 copies
questions.choice_C: Automatically grow or shrink a scaling factor based on detection of Inf/NaN overflows
questions.choice_D: Reorder matrix multiplications to reduce rounding error

questions.question: For gradient accumulation across multiple microbatches, what is a recommended precision strategy?
questions.choice_A: Accumulate gradients in FP16 to match the forward pass precision and save memory
questions.choice_B: Accumulate in FP32 to reduce summation error, even if individual microbatch gradients are computed in FP16/BF16
questions.choice_C: Accumulate in BF16 to maximize exponent range while preserving mantissa precision
questions.choice_D: Cast gradients to FP64 before accumulation to fully eliminate rounding error

questions.question: In Adam‑style optimizers, which precision choice is most critical to maintain training stability over long runs?
questions.choice_A: Storing parameters in FP16 while keeping gradients in FP32
questions.choice_B: Computing forward activations in FP16 while backprop in BF16
questions.choice_C: Clipping gradients in FP16 but computing loss in FP32
questions.choice_D: Keeping optimizer state (e.g., first and second moments) in FP32 even if params/activations use lower precision

questions.question: Which statement best reflects the typical impact of mixed‑precision on accuracy and convergence when implemented correctly?
questions.choice_A: With appropriate loss scaling and selective high‑precision ops, mixed‑precision can match FP32 accuracy and convergence
questions.choice_B: Mixed‑precision always converges faster but to a worse final accuracy than FP32
questions.choice_C: Mixed‑precision generally requires doubling the number of training steps to reach FP32 accuracy
questions.choice_D: Mixed‑precision eliminates the need for careful hyperparameter tuning

questions.question: How does PyTorch AMP’s autocast typically decide which dtype to use for an operation?
questions.choice_A: It forces all operations into the lowest precision supported by the device to maximize throughput
questions.choice_B: It keeps the entire forward graph in FP32 unless the user manually annotates layers
questions.choice_C: It maintains a per‑op whitelist/blacklist policy informed by kernel numerics and accumulates in higher precision when needed
questions.choice_D: It deterministically chooses BF16 for convolutions and FP16 for GEMMs on all hardware

questions.question: When is BF16 particularly attractive compared to FP16 during training?
questions.choice_A: When the primary concern is mantissa precision for representing very small gradients
questions.choice_B: When avoiding loss scaling and overflow/underflow issues is a priority and hardware has native BF16 support
questions.choice_C: When using CPUs without vector instructions
questions.choice_D: When tensor cores are disabled and only scalar ALUs are available

questions.question: Which description best captures the tradeoff between compute precision and accumulation precision within a GEMM on modern GPUs?
questions.choice_A: Both compute and accumulation must be in the same precision to ensure determinism
questions.choice_B: Low‑precision compute with low‑precision accumulation is preferred for stability
questions.choice_C: High‑precision compute with low‑precision accumulation is the typical configuration
questions.choice_D: Low‑precision multiply with higher‑precision accumulation preserves partial sums while retaining speed

questions.question: What problem does loss scaling primarily address in FP16 training?
questions.choice_A: Underflow of small gradients due to limited dynamic range; scaling multiplies the loss to move gradients into representable range
questions.choice_B: Overflow of activations in residual connections due to large batch sizes
questions.choice_C: Gradient noise introduced by dropout layers
questions.choice_D: Non‑determinism from asynchronous kernel launches

questions.question: How should gradient clipping be integrated with loss scaling in mixed‑precision training?
questions.choice_A: Clip gradients before unscaling to avoid additional casts
questions.choice_B: Apply clipping to the loss value rather than the gradients when scaling is enabled
questions.choice_C: Unscale gradients first, then perform clipping in the target norm domain, and finally step the optimizer
questions.choice_D: Clip only FP32 master weights to avoid overflow

questions.question: What is a common pitfall when extending AMP to custom CUDA kernels?
questions.choice_A: Autocast always casts inputs to FP64 for custom ops, causing slowdowns
questions.choice_B: Failure to implement or register autocast rules can force unnecessary up/downcasts or unsafe low‑precision execution
questions.choice_C: Custom ops cannot run under AMP and must be disabled during training
questions.choice_D: Custom ops invalidate dynamic loss scaling heuristics in the framework

questions.question: Regarding checkpoints and deployment, which practice maximizes reproducibility and flexibility?
questions.choice_A: Saving only the FP16 weights to minimize storage and loading time
questions.choice_B: Saving both FP16 and BF16 copies of all weights in a single checkpoint
questions.choice_C: Converting optimizer states to FP16 at save time to reduce disk usage
questions.choice_D: Saving FP32 master weights and optimizer states; cast for inference as needed

questions.question: Which sequence correctly describes gradient accumulation with loss scaling across N microbatches?
questions.choice_A: Scale each microbatch loss, backprop, accumulate gradients in FP32, unscale once before the optimizer step, then step
questions.choice_B: Backprop unscaled loss for the first microbatch and scaled losses for the remaining ones
questions.choice_C: Scale the loss only on the last microbatch to match the effective batch size
questions.choice_D: Unscale after every microbatch to avoid overflow detection noise

questions.question: What is the benefit of stochastic rounding when applying low‑precision updates?
questions.choice_A: It guarantees deterministic training across runs
questions.choice_B: It increases exponent range without changing the format
questions.choice_C: It reduces bias in rounding small updates, improving long‑horizon optimization stability
questions.choice_D: It eliminates the need for FP32 master weights

questions.question: Under autocast policies, which operations are typically executed in higher precision to improve numerical stability?
questions.choice_A: All pointwise activations and elementwise adds
questions.choice_B: Reductions and normalization statistics such as softmax, log‑sum‑exp, and batch norm mean/variance
questions.choice_C: Convolutions and GEMMs exclusively
questions.choice_D: Embedding lookups and gather/scatter ops

questions.question: Which runtime signal most strongly suggests that dynamic loss scaling needs to reduce the scale factor?
questions.choice_A: A gradual decrease in training accuracy over epochs
questions.choice_B: Increased host‑to‑device transfer time
questions.choice_C: A small rise in validation loss after learning rate warmup
questions.choice_D: Frequent Inf/NaN gradients detected during backprop at the current scale

questions.question: In distributed data‑parallel training with mixed precision, which approach balances bandwidth savings with numerical robustness?
questions.choice_A: Accumulate and unscale gradients in FP32 locally; optionally compress to FP16/BF16 only for communication with error compensation
questions.choice_B: Always communicate gradients in FP16 and keep no FP32 copies to avoid redundancy
questions.choice_C: Communicate gradients in FP64 to guarantee identical updates across ranks
questions.choice_D: Perform the all‑reduce on FP16 gradients before unscaling to reduce overflow risk

questions.question: When choosing between FP16 and BF16 for a very deep transformer prone to activation outliers, which is generally preferable and why?
questions.choice_A: FP16, because it has higher mantissa precision and avoids the need for loss scaling
questions.choice_B: FP16, because its exponent range matches FP32 and better accommodates outliers
questions.choice_C: BF16, because its FP32‑like exponent range reduces overflow/underflow risk and often removes the need for loss scaling
questions.choice_D: Either is equivalent; the decision has no impact on convergence behavior
